10009-wild-northern-scenes-or-sporting-a:
S. H. Hammond's 1857 book gathers sporting adventures with rifle and rod in the wilderness between the St. Lawrence and Lake Champlain. Dedicated to a friend who had floated its lakes and rivers, it celebrates a broad country of forest, water, and game.

Chapters follow hunting and fishing trips, including a fierce bear attack in which the hunter's knife met the animal's prongs above his knee. Hammond writes with a sportsman's relish for camp, trail, and shot. Readers get mid-nineteenth-century American outdoor life, before railroads and resorts tamed the northern woods.
10051-the-little-pilgrim-further-experie:
Margaret Oliphant's Little Pilgrim returns in these further experiences, after arriving lately on the other side, among those who know trouble and sorrow no more. Her heart, full of pity for the suffering, soon fills with questions and longing thoughts even amid happiness.

Those who care for the younger brethren, the simple ones of heaven, are touched by her questions, and her story follows what she learns of the new life. Oliphant writes tenderly about heaven as a place of work, wonder, and love. Readers get a gentle sequel, comforting rather than frightening, about life after death.
10633-the-history-of-the-rise-progress-a:
Thomas Clarkson, who had campaigned against the slave trade since his Cambridge prize essay of 1785, wrote this history of how Britain's Parliament came to abolish it. The volume, in an 1839 edition, is dedicated to the ministers whose government carried abolition, and to the memory of William Pitt. Clarkson tells the campaign from inside, as one of its leaders.

Chapters follow petitions, evidence, debates, and setbacks across two decades, naming allies and opponents alike. The book is both history and testimony, written by a man who lived the struggle. Readers get the fullest firsthand account of how the British slave trade was ended by law.
11431-character-sketches-of-romance-fict:
Edited by Marion Harland, volume one of Character Sketches of Romance, Fiction and the Drama. a revised American edition of Brewer's Reader's Handbook published in 1892, identifies characters from literature and drama for readers who meet a name without its story. Illustrations include Ichabod Crane, Constance de Beverley, Lady Bountiful, Sydney Carton, Bernhardt as Cleopatra, Captain Cuttle. Elaine, and the Ancient Mariner, with wood engravings of Abelard, Aeneas, Alberich, Antigone, Antony, and many others.

Brewer's handbook was a Victorian reference staple, answering who is who across novels, plays, and poems. Harland's revision Americanizes it for a new audience. The volume works as a browsing companion to nineteenth-century reading, useful whenever a character's origin has slipped from memory.
11858-george-washington-farmer-being-an-:
Paul Leland Haworth's George Washington, Farmer presents Washington at Mount Vernon, in home life and agricultural work, rather than on battlefields or in the presidency. The study draws on letters and papers, some of which, including a ciphering book and rules of civility, were sold in 1849 for twenty thousand dollars.

Haworth follows Washington's care for servants and land alike. He notes that the president wrote in 1794 that Old Bishop, an enslaved man, must be taken care of whether he went or stayed. The book's value lies in its domestic scale: farming, household management, and personal relations, showing a founder as a working planter whose daily decisions shaped his estate.
11943-the-winning-of-the-west-volume-3-t:
Volume 3 of Theodore Roosevelt's Winning of the West, subtitled The Founding of the Trans-Alleghany Commonwealths, 1784 to 1790, with a map, continues the Presidential Edition. Its preface notes that the material is that mentioned in the preface to the first volume, linking the three books as a single history.

Roosevelt traces how frontier settlements beyond the mountains became organized commonwealths, with governments, laws. Militias of their own, in the years between the Revolution and the new federal Constitution. The volume shows settlers turning camps and stations into states, a process Roosevelt treats as the political counterpart of the fighting described in earlier volumes.
12062-lighted-to-lighten-the-hope-of-ind:
Alice B. Van Doren published this study in 1922 after years of mission and school work in India. Written for women readers and study groups, it describes the daily lives of Indian women and girls across caste, faith, and region, from village homes to new colleges.

Chapters follow child marriage, widowhood, temple service, purdah, and the slow spread of schooling for girls, with portraits of students at Lucknow and Madras and medical trainees at Vellore. The book shows education, health care, and paid work already changing what Indian women could expect from life. The book reads now as both a record of its time and a plea for Indian women to lead that change themselves.
12324-the-elizabethan-parish-in-its-eccl:
Sedley Lynch Ware wrote this Johns Hopkins University study in 1908, as numbers seven and eight of series twenty-six on historical and political science. Ware, a fellow in history, examines the Elizabethan parish in its church and financial life.

Chapters treat the parish importance in local government, archdeacons courts, churchwardens duties, ministers duties, and obligations exacted from parishioners. Evidence comes from act books of judicial administration, injunctions, and oaths, including the oath parsons gave to churchwardens. Ware shows the parish as a unit of rule, not just worship: it taxed, policed morals, and kept records. The study is a careful piece of early modern local history.
12428-the-history-of-the-rise-progress-a:
Thomas Clarkson published this first volume of his History of the Rise, Progress, and Accomplishment of the Abolition of the African Slave-Trade in London in 1808. Clarkson, a leading abolitionist, dedicated the work to Grenville, Grey, Moira, Spencer, Holland, Erskine, and Ellenborough.

The volume traces the campaign against the slave trade from early pamphlets and Quaker testimony through parliamentary committees and public petitions. A mid-book passage weighs which of two evils the committee should select as its object, since the same end would follow either way. Clarkson writes as a participant historian, naming allies and opponents. The book is a founding text of abolition history, written by the man who organized it.
12492-recent-tendencies-in-ethics-three-:
W. R. Sorley, Knightbridge Professor of Moral Philosophy, gave these three lectures to clergy at Cambridge, published in 1904. Titles are Characteristics, Ethics and Evolution, and Ethics and Idealism. Sorley surveys English ethical thought of the last century, noting its limited range and its regard for facts.

Controversy centred, he says, on two questions: the origin of moral ideas and the criterion of moral value. Evolution and idealism then press those questions in new forms. Sorley writes for clergy who must preach morality in a scientific age, clear and academic in tone. The lectures offer a compact, period view of ethics at the turn of the century.
12507-the-history-of-the-rise-progress-a:
Thomas Clarkson's 1808 history tells how the British Parliament abolished the African slave trade. Chapter one continues from June 1788 to July 1789, as Clarkson travels to collect evidence, faces difficulty obtaining it, forms committees, and watches the Privy Council resume examinations and inspect African productions.

Witnesses for the cause go unexamined, a report is prepared and laid before the Commons, and twelve propositions follow. Opponents demand new evidence. Clarkson, a leading campaigner, writes as one who took part, and as historian. The book remains a key source for the campaign, detailed, partisan and proud of a moral victory won by evidence and persistence.
12692-the-high-school-captain-of-the-tea:
In this Gridley sequel Dick Prescott captains the school's athletic teams and must lead more than games. A revolt over the quarterback spot, a sneak's tricks, and a town slow to back school sport all test his nerve. Football, track, and a final charge for the town's pride fill the chapters.

Dick learns that a captain's job is to steady others, even when two star players are lost before a big match. Dave Darrin and Tom Reade back him through rain, doubt, and rival schools. The story keeps Hancock's brisk pace and plain moral: lead by example, and play the gentleman's game.
12696-john-smith-u-s-a:
Eugene Field's John Smith U.S.A., published in 1905, is introduced as the work of a genius rare and quaint, in childlike simplicity. Field, poet of keen perception and rare discrimination, stands in the introduction beside Artemus Ward, Mark Twain, Bill Nye, Riley, Opie Read and Bret Harte in their happiest moods.

A poetic vein, workable in any direction, let Field extract what imagination saw and felt most. Though he longed to linger in the child-world, he wandered among older children, where listeners follow him into a temple of mirth. The book gathers Field's humorous and sentimental pieces about an ordinary American, John Smith, in verse and prose.
12774-dave-darrin-s-first-year-at-annapo:
H. Irving Hancock's boys' adventure opens as Dave Darrin and Dan Dalzell arrive as plebes at the United States Naval Academy. Their first year brings hazing, drill, class rivalry, and the unwritten code that rules midshipman life. Fights, pranks, and scrapes test whether the two friends can hold their nerve and their honour.

Dave, the steadier of the pair, learns to stand up to bullies without breaking the rules that bind the corps. Dan supplies jokes and trouble in near equal measure. The story moves from the exam rooms to the parade ground and the boxing ring, offering young readers a lively, clean picture of Annapolis training.
13068-twenty-one-days-in-india-or-the-to:
George R. Aberigh-Mackay's Twenty-One Days in India, ninth edition 1914, reprints his Vanity Fair papers as the tour of Sir Ali Baba. The papers first ran in 1879, and this edition adds Bombay Gazette pieces signed Our Political Orphan. Aberigh-Mackay, once principal of Rajkumar College at Indore, writes satire, not a guidebook.

His targets include the collector, whom he calls the automaton of empire, while the secretariat is its consciousness. To most Indians, he says, the collector is the government itself. Other sketches mock traveling MPs, shy scholars, and the whole parade of Anglo-Indian life. The book is witty, sharp, and still quoted for its view of how the Raj saw itself.
13119-jean-franc-ois-millet-a-collection:
Estelle M. Hurll's 1900 Riverside Art Series volume presents fifteen pictures by Jean-François Millet, with a portrait of the painter and her own introduction and notes. Hurll opens with Millet's character as an artist, adds books of reference, a directory of the pictures, and a table of his life. The aim is to help general readers look, not just glance.

She reads The Sower and other works for their sense of motion, then turns indoors to The Knitting Lesson, where peasant girls learn plain needlework early. A later picture shows children at play with rude home-made toys, watched by a smiling mother at the door. Hurll's notes make Millet's peasant world clear and human, picture by picture.
1318-the-twin-hells-a-thrilling-narrativ:
John N. Reynolds, who served sixteen months in the Kansas penitentiary and time in Missouri's, tells what he saw inside: the cells, the stripes, the labor, and the cruelty of the keepers. His narrative names names and spares no detail of the twin hells of his title.

Reynolds writes as a witness and a reformer, urging readers to end the abuses he suffered. The book is raw, angry, and firsthand. It stands as a document of American prison life in the nineteenth century, and it still shocks with its plain testimony.
13229-the-revelation-explained-an-exposi:
F. G. Smith's Revelation Explained expounds John's Apocalypse text by text. It traces prophecy from Patmos through Christian growth, Mohammedanism in the east, the papacy in the west, and Protestantism, to the final judgment. Smith, author of What the Bible Teaches, quotes Isaiah: former things are come to pass, and new things God declares before they spring forth.

Smith reads witnesses in sackcloth, saints ground by proud oppressors, and a voice declaring they have shed saints' blood and must drink blood in turn. He also cites an 1812 book, Truth Advocated, by Theophilus Gates, borrowed from a neighbor in Michigan. The exposition is thorough, confident, and shaped by Smith's church tradition, verse by verse.
13268-hindu-literature-comprising-the-bo:
Edited by Epiphanius Wilson in a revised 1900 edition, Hindu Literature gathers the Book of Good Counsels, Nala and Damayanti, the Ramayana, and Sakuntala, with critical and biographical sketches. The Book of Good Counsels opens with the winning of friends, through tales of a jackal, deer, and crow, and a vulture, cat, and birds. Each fable teaches prudence through beasts.

Nala's tale turns on gods who offer a mortal woman heavenly robes and unfading wreaths, urging her to choose a god over a man. Sakuntala's story closes with a father urging patience on daughters who kept their father's honor, calling patience alms, truth, and sacrifice. The volume is a broad English door into Sanskrit story and epic.
1333-robert-f-murray-author-of-the-scarl:
Andrew Lang, the Scots man of letters, writes a memoir of Robert F. Murray, a young St. Andrews poet who died at twenty-nine, and gathers his poems beside it. Murray's verse, touched by the university town and by illness, is light, learned, and melancholy.

Lang's memoir gives the poems their human frame: a brief life, a circle of friends, and a promise cut short. The volume preserves a minor poet who might else be lost. It suits readers who like Victorian verse and the friendship of letters. Lang's memoir preserves a young poet who might else be lost.
13331-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
Hubert C. Corlette's 1901 Cathedral Church of Chichester, in Bell's Cathedrals series, gives a short history and description of the fabric, with an account of the diocese and see, and forty-five illustrations. Corlette leans on Professor Willis's architectural history, Precentor Walcott's early statutes, and Dean Stephen's diocesan history. The book is a compact guide for visitors.

He traces how builders, needing more light, made window arches more varied and mouldings more delicate than the stronger, deeper-cut types before them. Later, he notes a gable window not yet restored, soon to vanish by decay, and a blocked window above it. The volume is careful, scholarly, and useful for anyone walking Chichester's aisles.
13536-notes-and-queries-index-of-volume-:
An index to the first volume of Notes and Queries, November 1849 to May 1850, lists the journal's opening half-year in alphabetical order. Abbey of St. Wandrille, abdication of James II, Aberdeen's Burnet prize, aboriginal chambers near Tilbury, and emancipation of the Jews open the A entries, each with page references.

Later pages cover bells, Coleridge's Christabel and Byron's Lara, pet names, charms, havior, emeralds, and eminent Englishmen, with Milton's minor poems, misquotations, mistakes in Gibbon, and Gray's elegy among the M entries. The index makes the first volume searchable, turning scattered letters into a reference tool for antiquaries and literary readers.
13600-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
A slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, published in twenty-nine volumes in 1910 and 1911. This volume carries the alphabet from Andros to the start of the A entries in volume two. Hundreds of signed articles by specialists cover history, biography, science, literature, and the arts, each with sources for further reading.

Readers meet figures such as Sir Edmund Andros and statesmen of the age, alongside entries on places, peoples, and ideas of the time. The writing keeps a firm, factual tone, with dates, careers, and context given in compact form. As a reference work it shows what educated readers of 1910 were told about the world, and it still serves as a check on names, events, and terms from that era.
13748-have-faith-in-massachusetts-2d-ed-:
Calvin Coolidge, governor of Massachusetts, collected his speeches and messages in Have Faith in Massachusetts. This second, enlarged edition adds later addresses to the first. Coolidge argues for sound community life, honest government, and respect for law. He defends property, service, and the rewards of work in plain, pithy sentences.

An introductory note praises his clear thinking and gift for short expression. Speeches cover rights, duties, education, and public morals. Coolidge holds that one right cannot survive if another is violated. The collection shows the style that later carried him to the presidency. It remains a key source for Coolidge's early political thought.
13954-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for June 27, 1917, is a wartime number with calendar, cartoons, and stories. A full calendar for 1917 fronts the issue, month by month. Later pages follow a factory fire, where burning coal dragged from a furnace sets inflammable material alight. Workers rush to alarm, and Mignon, gone out to earn her living, reappears in the tale.

Punch's wartime humour mixes domestic drama with satire. The issue is shorter than peacetime numbers, reflecting paper shortage. Cartoons and short fiction carry the comedy. Readers get a snapshot of Britain in the third war year. The number suits collectors of Punch and war humour.
13988-fugitive-slave-law-the-religious-d:
Ichabod S. Spencer preached this sermon on the religious duty of obedience to law in Brooklyn on November 24, 1850. Published by M. W. Dodd, it answers the Fugitive Slave Law from a pro-obedience pulpit. Congregants, including Jasper Corning and Francis H. Abbott, requested a copy for publication the next day. Spencer argues rulers are ministers of God for good.

He quotes Paul: rulers are not a terror to good works, but to evil, and Christians must be subject for conscience' sake. The sermon defends law and order against abolitionist disobedience. It shows Northern clergy divided over the 1850 compromise. The text suits students of religion and slavery. Its argument stands in sharp contrast to Child and Hossack.
15134-supplement-to-animal-sanctuaries-i:
Lieutenant-Colonel William Wood issued this 1912 supplement to his address on animal sanctuaries in Labrador, for Canada's Commission of Conservation. A year earlier he had urged protection for Labrador wildlife; this follow-up gathers the response from press, scientists, and sportsmen across the English-speaking world.

Review copies had gone out by the thousand, and Wood reports a warm welcome from zoological journals, sporting magazines, and animal welfare papers. The supplement sets the case on firmer ground with advice and criticism from experts. It marks an early step toward wildlife refuges in Canada's far north.
15478-new-york-times-current-history-the:
This April 1915 number of Current History, the New York Times monthly magazine, opens volume two of its European War record. It mixes German decrees, maps, poems, and essays, giving American readers the war as it unfolded, with documents and commentary side by side. The issue starts at page one, with Germany's war zone and neutral flags.

Articles cover Germany's submarine war, a German case on starving out the enemy answered by sixteen specialists, and Zeppelin raids on London. Poems include Reveille by John Galsworthy and The Peace of the World by H. G. Wells, while a hymn of hatred, God Punish England, Brother, shows German feeling at its fiercest. The number is a raw archive of 1915 opinion, before later histories settled its judgments.
15565-sir-john-constantine-memoirs-of-hi:
A. T. Quiller-Couch, as Q, edited these memoirs of Sir John Constantine, written by his son Prosper Paleologus, otherwise Constantine. The memoirs begin in 1756 and follow adventures at home and abroad, particularly in Corsica. An epigraph on knighthood sets the theme: knighthood lies not in fighting for right or wrong, but in a cause truth cannot deny, with justice mixed with mercy.

Chapters trace lineage, a pilgrimage, a kingdom acquired, a father building an army from nothing and planning an invasion in five minutes, and a company of the rose. A landing on an island, enchantment wasting an army without fighting, and a hostage to Princess Camilla follow. The editor notes that many episodes, sermons, and digressions were cut. The book is a playful historical romance, chivalrous, comic, and fond of its own inventions.
15612-genesis-a:
Lawrence Mason taught English at Yale College. He translated Genesis A from the Old English. Henry Holt published it in New York in 1915, as number 48 of Yale Studies in English, edited by Albert Cook. Mason argues that to translate is to modernize, and refuses an artificial, pseudo-antique hybrid. He aims at literal fidelity in idiomatic modern literary English, without conscious mannerisms.

Mason keeps the original's explosive appositions, asyndeton, and synonymy. He does not smooth them into easy, flowing modern sentences. That smoothing would sacrifice the poem's force. The poem retells Genesis in Anglo-Saxon verse: creation, the fall, and the patriarchs, in the heroic style of early English poetry. The volume gives students and general readers a readable Genesis A, with the strangeness of its Old English rhetoric intact.
16423-a-coal-from-the-altar-to-kindle-th:
Sam Ward, Bachelor of Divinity, preaches holy zeal in this early Puritan sermon, reprinted in modern type. The title image says it all: a coal from the altar to kindle sacred fire in the reader's heart. Ward writes for Christians who feel their faith grown cold and need fresh heat for duty and devotion.

The sermon is short, fiery, and direct, in the plain Puritan style of pulpit exhortation. It belongs to a world of fasts, sermons, and earnest self-searching. Readers of early English religious prose will find a compact sample of Puritan preaching at its most ardent.
17306-the-condition-of-the-working-class:
Frederick Engels wrote this study of English workers in 1844, and this edition pairs it with a preface he wrote in 1892. Florence Kelley Wischnewetzky's translation was printed in London by George Allen and Unwin. Engels argues that the steam engine and cotton machinery sparked an industrial revolution that remade civil society. England, its classic soil, is the place to study its chief product, the proletariat.

The book walks through factory towns, housing, wages, health, and daily life, drawing on reports and on what Engels saw himself. Its claim is stark: a new working class had been made by machines, and its condition was the great question of the age. Readers still meet here the founding text of modern social criticism, plain in its anger and rich in detail.
17511-foch-the-man-a-life-of-the-supreme:
Clara E. Laughlin wrote this life of Marshal Foch, supreme commander of the Allied armies. It is a revised and enlarged edition, with an appreciation by Lieutenant-Colonel Edouard Requin of the French High Commission to the United States. A frontispiece shows Marshal Foch at the Peace Conference. The book follows him from birth and boyhood surroundings to command.

Chapters cover the horse markets at Tarbes, the school, and Foch at twelve as a student of Napoleon. A young soldier of a lost cause recalls what Foch suffered in France's defeat by the Prussians. Paris after the Germans left finds him beginning military studies, determined to be ready when France needed him. Readers get a wartime biography, admiring and accessible.
17619-a-jongleur-strayed-verses-on-love-:
Richard Le Gallienne published this book of verses on love and other matters, sacred and profane, with an introduction by Oliver Herford, in a Garden City, New York, edition. The contents mix an echo from Horace, a ballade of the oldest duel in the world, sorcery, and the dryad. They also include May is back, moon-marketing, two birthdays, a song, the faithful lover, and love's tenderness.

Le Gallienne, a poet of the 1890s, writes in a light, musical manner, fond of old forms and romantic feeling. Readers get a late collection from a poet whose fame had peaked a generation earlier. The book suits readers of light verse and of the aesthetic movement's afterlife.
18033-the-boston-terrier-and-all-about-i:
Edward Axtell wrote The Boston Terrier and All About It as a practical, scientific guide to the American dog, printed in Battle Creek in a fourth edition in 1910. Axtell ran the St. Botolph Kennels in Massachusetts, and he served the Boston Terrier Club for twelve years.

Chapters cover the breed, its club, its standard, kenneling, breeding, and care, with the club's rules and official marks laid out in full. Axtell writes as a breeder who loves his dogs and knows his trade. The book stays useful for terrier fans, and it shows how a new American breed won its place in the dog world.
18209-english-seamen-in-the-sixteenth-ce:
James Anthony Froude, late Regius Professor of Modern History at Oxford, gave these lectures in the Easter terms of 1893 and 1894. Froude opens with Jean Paul's jest that God gave France the empire of the land, England the empire of the sea, and Germany the empire of the air. England, he says, still held her watery dominion. From that sea power, the English race had spread across the globe.

Lectures follow the sea cradle of the Reformation and John Hawkins and the African slave trade. They cover Hawkins and Philip II, Drake's voyage round the world, parties in the state, and the great expedition to the West Indies. They close with the attack on Cadiz and the sailing and defeat of the Armada. Readers get Tudor sea power told as a story of sailors, faith, and empire.
18250-the-prose-works-of-jonathan-swift-:
Volume seven of Jonathan Swift's prose works, edited by Temple Scott for Bohn's Standard Library, gathers his historical and Irish writings. The London, Cambridge, New York, and Bombay edition places Swift in Dublin from 1714. It follows the fall of the Harley administration, when Harley lay in the Tower and Bolingbroke lived in exile in France. Swift met jeers, suspicion, and polite indifference from his clerical colleagues.

Contents include a letter on choosing a new speaker in Ireland. They also give a proposal for the universal use of Irish manufacture, an essay on English bubbles, the Swearer's Bank, and a short view of the state of Ireland. The story of the injured lady and answers to memorials of the Irish poor follow. Readers get Swift as Irish patriot and satirist, writing for a country he served with anger and wit.
18288-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
The Northern Nut Growers Association met at Rochester, New York, on September 1 and 2, 1915, and this volume prints the proceedings of its sixth annual meeting. It opens with officers and committees, members, the constitution, and the by-laws, then gives the secretary-treasurer's report and the papers read at the meeting.

The papers cover forest conditions in New York and new tree crops and a new agriculture. Other papers give notes on hazels, northern pecan trees, and walnut observations in California. They also cover pruning the Persian walnut and nut growing in Canada. An appendix lists those present. Growers get a practical record of trials, kinds, and methods, and a picture of a young field learning by shared trial.
19050-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
This volume records the eighth annual meeting of the Northern Nut Growers Association, held at Stamford, Connecticut, on September 5 and 6, 1917. It prints the constitution, by-laws, and papers read by growers and researchers. A disclaimer warns that views are the authors' own, not the association's.

Rules set fees, committees on hybrids and seedlings, and votes for change, while papers weigh nut kinds, soils, and growing methods. Pesticide advice is dated and must not be followed without current labels. Readers get a period record of early American nut growing as a shared craft and science.
19373-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
This volume records the tenth annual meeting of the Northern Nut Growers Association, held at Battle Creek, Michigan, on December 9 and 10, 1919. President W. C. Reed of Vincennes presided in the Battle Creek Sanitarium annex, opening with a short business session and his address. A disclaimer warns that papers are the authors' own.

Rules on committees, fees, and amendments repeat the association's constitution, while papers weigh nut kinds and growing methods. Pesticide advice is dated and must not be followed without current labels. Readers get a period record of American nut growing after the First World War.
19503-historic-tales-the-romance-of-real:
Charles Morris wrote this third volume of his Historic Tales, on Spanish America, published in Philadelphia and London in the early nineteen hundreds. It opens with the departure of Columbus, then follows Cortez at Vera Cruz, Aztec idols, the death of Atahualpa, and scenes from Panama to Rio.

Freebooters crossing unknown country with sick comrades and prisoners in tow give one tale its hard edge. Morris tells conquest and settlement as vivid story, with pictures of rivers, harbors, and native crafts to match. Balboa's discovery of the Pacific and Coronado's hunt for the Seven Cities of Cibola get tales of their own.
19511-bell-s-cathedrals-wimborne-minster:
Thomas Perkins wrote this double guide to Wimborne Minster and Christchurch Priory for Bell's cathedral series, with pictures from his own photographs. Each church gets a history of its building, a walk round its outside, and a tour of its inside, with tables of measures for the curious.

Christchurch closes with deans, priors, and vicars, while Wimborne adds St. Margaret's Hospital to its story. Perkins writes in the series' plain style, and the volume still helps visitors read two Dorset churches stone by stone. At Christchurch the tour pauses at the Lady Chapel and its storied miraculous beam, plus the Shelley monument.
19728-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
Nut growers in the northern United States formed an association to share craft knowledge. Its reports record proceedings, papers, and member lists. One surviving page lists pomologists from the Department of Agriculture in Washington. Names like Professor C. P. Close and Walter Van Fleet appear among them. Van Fleet was a noted plant breeder of the era.

Northern nut growing faced cold winters that southern growers escaped. Chestnuts, walnuts, and hickories needed hardy strains and patient testing. Association reports spread results that no single farm could gather. They list who grew what, and where. For farm historians, such lists are gold. They show American horticulture organizing itself, name by name.
19859-a-flat-iron-for-a-farthing-or-some:
Juliana Horatia Ewing wrote A Flat Iron for a Farthing, passages in the life of an only son. When children clamor for a story, the narrator's wife sends them to him. Tell them how you bought a flat iron for a farthing, she says. He is glad to tell it for three reasons. It is about himself, someone dear, and his own childhood. The tale unfolds as family storytelling.

Ewing was among the finest Victorian writers for children. Her only son narrates with humor and exact memory. A farthing's purchase becomes an epic of childhood economy. Grown readers find real feeling under the comedy. The book influenced later masters of children's fiction. It deserves its classic standing.
20200-christmas-a-happy-time-a-tale-calc:
Christmas: A Happy Time is a tale made for the amusement of young readers. Harriet warns that some hoped-for guests will never come at last. She reminds the others not to open the gate outside. Papa and mamma have both forbidden it, she says with care.

The children shiver in a sharp, cutting wind by that gate. Harriet urges a run round the garden to get warm again. Mamma has begged them not to stand still in such cold. Young readers get a crisp Christmas scene of waiting, hope, and home rules.
20221-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
Northern Nut Growers Association reports record yearly meetings of growers and experts. This volume lists members from Nebraska to Ohio and beyond. William Caha of Wahoo and Ward M. Canaday of Toledo appear. Arthur S. Colby of the University of Illinois is also listed.

Such rolls show a wide, keen network behind American nut growing. Reports held talks, elections, and notes on trees and yields as well. Their value now lies in names, places, and dated facts. Readers tracing farm history or family names may find gold here. Growers shared seed, grafts, and hard-won lessons through these yearly gatherings.
20532-love-among-the-chickens-a-story-of:
P. G. Wodehouse published Love Among the Chickens in 1908, subtitled a story of the haps and mishaps on an English chicken farm. The narrator, Jeremy Garnet, is dragged down to Devon by his friend Ukridge. Ukridge plans to make a fortune raising chickens, a subject he knows nothing about.

Garnet reports the scheme's collapse with dry alarm. It is highly improbable, he says, that Ukridge will ever grow old if he repeats his last night's performance. The book mixes farm chaos with a love affair, in the comic style that soon made Wodehouse famous.
20851-character-sketches-of-romance-fict:
Mark Tapley, jolly through every hardship in Martin Chuzzlewit, stars in one sketch here. Dickens's man finds no credit in cheer when life runs smooth. Fever, fraud, and loss in Eden test his creed to the full.

Character Sketches of Romance, Fiction, and the Drama gathers famed figures in short accounts. E. B. Brewer's Reader's Handbook stands behind this vast, handy set. Volume three runs through plays, poems, and novels in alphabetical order. Readers once kept such sets by the desk to place a name or trace a tale in seconds.
20903-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
Connecticut names lead the roll in the Northern Nut Growers Association report. Tree experts, doctors, and growers from Stamford to Hartford fill the list. Their meeting papers treat the nuts that thrive in northern soils.

Chestnut, walnut, hickory, and filbert culture fills reports like this one in full detail. Growers swap notes on blight, grafts, soil, and yields by state. The group pushed nut trees as farm crops and shade plantings alike. These proceedings keep the craft of a niche farming world, exact and earnest, for growers and tree lovers to mine.
20915-field-s-chromatography-or-treatise:
Fresh hues on the walls of Theban tombs prove how old the science of colour runs. Field's Chromatography, a treatise on colours and pigments, opens with that deep past. Royal tomb paintings stayed so fresh, it says, as to need no repair.

George Field spent his life on pigments that would not fade or turn. Artists' colours, their making, and their faults fill his famed guide. Later editors rewrote and updated it for new generations of painters. The book stands as a bridge of craft, where chemistry serves art in the studio, colour by tested colour.
20938-stops-or-how-to-punctuate-a-practi:
Commas do too much work, charges Paul Allardyce in Stops, or How to Punctuate. Their vague use, he says, truly harms English style in our time. A firmer system for the old marks would pay at once, he argues.

Allardyce sets out each stop's right work in a practical handbook for writers. Comma, colon, dash, and full stop each get rules and cases. Students and clerks of the pen stood to gain most from its order. The book shows an age that prized clear prose taking its smallest tools with full gravity, mark by mark.
21190-expositions-of-holy-scripture-seco:
Alexander Maclaren, the great Manchester preacher, expounds six New Testament letters in this volume of his Expositions of Holy Scripture. It covers the end of Second Corinthians, Galatians, and Philippians in full, then Colossians, Thessalonians, and First Timothy. Each sermon takes a short text and opens it up.

Titles like Hope and Holiness, Rich Yet Poor, and Strength in Weakness show Maclaren's method. He takes a verse, gives a clear outline, and applies it closely to daily Christian life. He answers the charge that professing Christians often ignore common morality. These printed sermons let readers far from his pulpit study his preaching week by week.
21516-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
Growers of nut trees report their results in the Northern Nut Growers Association's printed proceedings. The reports carry the findings of each writer alone, not the backing of the group. A note warns that spray laws and advice may have changed since the papers were written.

Pages treat named kinds of nut trees, grafting, planting, and yields by district. A photo shows a Detroit grower standing under a fine tree, thanks to Gilbert Becker of Michigan. Members swap what worked in one soil and season, with no promise it will work elsewhere. For orchard keepers in cold states, the volume is a trove of trials.
21620-the-myth-of-hiawatha-and-other-ora:
Henry R. Schoolcraft gathers Indigenous tales in The Myth of Hiawatha, published at Philadelphia in 1856. He took the legends from the storytelling circle of the native wigwams. The book is dedicated to Longfellow, whose poem Hiawatha had just drawn on the same store.

Schoolcraft claims the tales show their tellers as they truly are. They reveal what the people believe, hope, fear, wish for, and worship. He argues they place Indigenous character in a wholly new light. As agent and scholar, Schoolcraft spent years among the Ojibwe and others, and his set remains a key, if dated, record.
21829-a-treatise-on-domestic-economy-for:
Running a home is a serious science in Catharine E. Beecher's Treatise on Domestic Economy, first issued in the 1840s for young ladies at home and school. Beecher blames poor health, poor servants, and faulty training for the wives whose strength failed in their first married years. Her book answers with method: health, order, and skill applied to every room of the house.

Chapters teach the care of health, food, children, servants, and the house itself, with engravings to guide the eye. Beecher dedicated the work to American mothers. It became one of the most used housekeeping books of its century. Modern readers find in it both practical lore and a clear window on women's work in 1845.
22094-travels-in-the-great-desert-of-sah:
James Richardson, an English traveller sent to open trade with the Sahara, crossed the great desert in 1845 and 1846. His Travels in the Great Desert of Sahara reports the journey from Tripoli toward the Sudan. Richardson apologises in his preface for the delayed map and commercial reports. The routes he surveyed were meant to guide British trade into the African interior.

He describes wells, caravans, Tuareg and Arab tribes, slavery, and the price of goods. The desert itself, its heat, sand, and thirst, dominates every chapter. Richardson later died on a second, grander expedition. His travels remain a basic source for the Sahara as Europeans first mapped it.
22200-recollections-with-photogravure-po:
David Christie Murray, a popular Victorian novelist, published his Recollections late in his career. The volume carries his portrait in photogravure and a preface of addresses. Murray begins with his birth on the thirteenth of April, which his mother called the unlucky day of the fool's month. He jokes that the phrase proved rich in prophetic wisdom about his life.

From a Birmingham childhood he rose through journalism to the London literary world. The Recollections roam over editors, actors, publishers, and the making of novels. Murray writes easily, with a professional's store of anecdote. His memoir is a useful, genial witness to the book trade of the late nineteenth century.
22238-charles-carleton-coffin-war-corres:
Charles Carleton Coffin was a Civil War correspondent, traveller, and author of boys' histories. This biography, published in 1898 near the end of his life, adds statesman to his titles. Its introduction says Coffin had a face that helped one believe in God. His whole life, the writer claims, was an evidence of Christianity, and he was an organiser of happiness who never sought riches.

Coffin reported Bull Run and a dozen other battles for Boston papers. Later his histories taught two generations of American boys their country's story. This life, written in warm admiration, records the reputation he left: the genial war correspondent who made history read like a story.
22260-bell-s-cathedrals-the-abbey-church:
H. J. L. J. Massé wrote this guide to Tewkesbury Abbey for Bell's Cathedral series. The little books in that series put a scholarly guide into a tourist's pocket. Massé thanks the owners of the Registrum Theokusburiae, the abbey's own register, for lending it for months. He also borrows plates on Saxon churches from the Archaeological Institute's journal, with leave.

Tewkesbury's great Norman tower and its tombs of princes fill the chapters. Massé traces the abbey from its founding through the Dissolution, when the townspeople bought their church to save it. The guide mixes architecture, history, and practical visiting notes. It is a model of the Edwardian church handbook.
22312-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
Growers who raised nut trees formed their own association and printed its proceedings. The Northern Nut Growers Association report records one such meeting. Its pages list members and officers by state and town.

The roll runs from Connecticut and Florida to Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio. Names appear from Panama's Canal Zone as well as Virginia and New York. That spread shows a young industry organizing itself across the country. Inside, readers find the working record of people trading knowledge on nut growing. It preserves names, places, and concerns of early American nut culture that would else be lost.
22400-fox-s-book-of-martyrs-or-a-history:
Fox's Book of Martyrs records the lives, sufferings, and deaths of Christian martyrs. John Foxe's great work stood in English homes beside the Bible for centuries. This edition carries his history of persecution onward.

Its preface argues that persecution is no one creed's vice. Intolerant Jew and bigoted pagan show the same spirit, it says. So do the nominal Christian, the infidel, and the atheist. The urge to force belief is called an inherent vice of fallen nature. Men try to restrain hated opinions by physical pressure. They use the same pressure to spread favored ones. The accounts that follow test that claim in blood.
22460-new-york-times-current-history-the:
The New York Times Current History gathered war news into monthly volumes. Volume two, number five, covers the European War in early 1915. Its pages reprint official notices and reports as they arrived.

On February 4, the German Admiralty proclaimed a war zone. Every enemy merchant ship found around Great Britain would be destroyed. It would not always be possible, Germany warned, to save crews. Passengers, too, would face dangers that could not be averted. That chilling notice marked a turn toward submarine warfare without mercy. Readers today get the war as Americans first read it. It is history in the raw, before outcomes were known.
22471-the-fair-play-settlers-of-the-west:
George D. Wolf studied the Fair Play settlers of the West Branch Valley. Their years, 1769 to 1784, frame his study of frontier ethnography. These settlers governed themselves beyond Pennsylvania's official reach and law.

Wolf calls their story worth telling for one clear reason. It might offer insight into democracy's development on the frontier. His account is an ethnography of how these settlers lived and ruled. He warns it is not meant to typify all frontiers. It is simply an illustration, and he hopes a useful one. Readers get a close case study in self-government. Settlers made law where no law had been provided for them.
22589-jubilation-u-s-a:
Jubilation, U.S.A. is a science fiction story about alien visitors arriving in a very ordinary America. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. In the sample scene, two aliens halt on a road as a wheezing pre-war Chevy chokes its way toward them.

The visitors step into a gully beside the road, ready to run for their ship if the welcome turns hostile. They expect a friendly reception, but they are not sure of their figures. That mix of cosmic travel and small-town caution gives the story its dry comic tone. It belongs to the magazine tradition that played first contact for gentle satire rather than terror. Readers of classic short science fiction will enjoy its deadpan setup.
22721-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
The Northern Nut Growers Association Report of the Proceedings is a conference record from the society that promoted nut growing in northern North America. The catalog record names no editor and gives no year. Papers, discussions, and membership lists make up the volume, as in the association's other reports.

The surviving sample is a roll of members and contacts, state by state: Alabama, Alberta, British Columbia, California, Connecticut, and on through Manitoba, Mexico, and the New England states. Names like Dr. Colt in California and A. Hale in Alberta mark a network of growers swapping varieties and results. Proceedings of this kind carried the practical science of a niche crop. Orchard historians can trace from them how northern nut culture spread.
22831-as-a-chinaman-saw-us-passages-from:
America gets reviewed by a visitor in As a Chinaman Saw Us, a set of letters home from a Chinese traveler. He writes with dry care. The great powers, he notes, believe they are still evolving toward perfection, while Americans assure him the United States has already arrived. Criticizing such a finished nation, he jokes, takes real nerve.

That polite irony runs through the letters. Customs, manners, politics, and national pride all pass before a calm outsider's eye, and his praise often carries a sting. The book belongs to a small shelf of works that reversed the usual travel gaze of the period. It still reads freshly because its main tool, understatement, has not dated at all.
23656-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
The Northern Nut Growers Association held its third annual meeting at Lancaster, Pennsylvania, on December 18 and 19, 1912, and this volume, printed at Ithaca in 1913, records what happened there. Officers and committees open the proceedings, and the body of the book is the papers and discussions of growers, researchers, and orchardists.

Readers will find reports on nut tree cultivars, planting and care, pests, and the results of trials in different soils and climates. The book adds the plain caveat that what thrived in one place at one time may not thrive elsewhere. It is a working record of an early American effort to turn nut growing from a hobby into a reliable farm crop.
24527-fragments-of-science-a-series-of-d:
John Tyndall, the Irish physicist, gathered these essays, addresses, and reviews into Fragments of Science, published at London in 1879 in a sixth edition. The first volume treats inorganic nature: the constitution of nature, radiation, the aether, and the atomic theory.

Later essays cover absorption of radiant heat by gases and vapours, invisible rays, fog signals, Niagara, Alpine sculpture, and a voyage to Algeria to observe an eclipse. Tyndall writes with rare clarity about hard science for general readers. The volume remains a classic of Victorian popular science, by one of its great explainers.
24552-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
Published at Concord, New Hampshire, in 1914, this volume reports the fourth annual meeting of the Northern Nut Growers Association, held at Washington, D.C., on 18 and 19 November 1913. Its contents list officers, members, constitution, and the full proceedings of the meeting.

Papers cover Persian walnuts, forage nuts, chestnuts and walnuts in Europe, the chestnut blight, pecan top-working, and methods of propagating nut trees. Later papers treat nut-tree diseases, injurious insects, and nut culture in Utah. The volume preserves early American horticulture at work, and it still interests growers and historians of farming.
24559-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
Published at Concord, New Hampshire, in 1915, this volume reports the fifth annual meeting of the Northern Nut Growers Association, held at Evansville, Indiana, on 20 and 21 August 1914. Its contents list officers, members, constitution, and the proceedings of the meeting, with a secretary-treasurer's report.

Papers cover a score card for judging nuts, the status and possibilities of nut culture in the north, cultivation and fertilisers, and personal experiences with hybridising nut trees. Later discussion takes up grafting, varieties, and orchard care. The volume preserves a young science of nut growing, told by the growers themselves.
24629-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
Published after its meeting, this volume reports the eleventh annual meeting of the Northern Nut Growers Association, held at Washington, D.C., on 7 and 8 October 1920. Its contents list officers, state vice-presidents, members, and constitution, with the proceedings of the convention and a secretary-treasurer's report.

Papers cover chestnut work at the Bell experiment plot, nut culture in the United States, an address by David Fairchild, and the place of nut trees in northern culture. Later papers treat filberts, hickories, pecans, and insects that injure nuts. The volume preserves American nut growing as a young science, told by its workers.
24839-the-blonde-lady-being-a-record-of-:
Maurice Leblanc published this Lupin book in France in 1907, in an American edition of 1910 translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos. It records the duel of wits between Arsene Lupin, gentleman thief, and Holmlock Shears, the English detective, a name Leblanc used in England for Sherlock Holmes. Two episodes make up the book: The Blonde Lady and The Jewish Lamp.

The first opens with Professor Gerbois and a lottery ticket, number 514, series 23, then moves to a blue diamond, a kidnapping, and Lupin's second arrest. Shears and Wilson blunder through locked gates and dark clues while Lupin stays a step ahead. Fans of classic detective fiction will enjoy a brisk, witty contest of thief against sleuth.
24952-a-mona-the-child-and-the-beast-and:
Louis Becke's South Seas stories, drawn from 'The Strange Adventure of James Shervinton' and published by T. Fisher Unwin in 1902, center on Amona, a Niué cook in the service of the bully Armitage. The island world of traders, ships, and uneasy authority fills the background. The title tale turns on a hidden secret: the truth behind Armitage's wife's death and his child's lameness.

A second story, 'The Snake and the Bell,' shifts to Becke's own childhood at Mosman's Bay in Sydney, a quieter memory beside the Pacific tales. Together the pieces show Becke's range, from island intrigue to boyhood recollection, told in the plain, sea-going voice that made his name. The collection suits readers who like their adventure salted with real places.
25129-baboo-jabberjee-b-a:
F. Anstey's Baboo Jabberjee, B.A., published in London by J. M. Dent in the Wayfarer's Library, is a comic record of an Indian graduate loose in London society. Jabberjee, earnest and eager, writes up his adventures in gloriously tangled English, apologizing for his modest scope while offering confidences, criticisms, and complaints on every page.

He attends the Westminster Play, pronounces on the Laureateship and the Old Masters, tries bicycling, visits Olympia, orates at a ladies' debating club, and watches a glove fight. Anstey's joke cuts both ways: Jabberjee's blunders expose English snobbery as surely as they expose his own innocence, and the sketches still raise a smile.
25135-with-the-guards-brigade-from-bloem:
The Reverend E. P. Lowry's With the Guards' Brigade, published in London in 1902, records the Boer War from a chaplain's side. Lowry served as senior Wesleyan chaplain with the South African Field Force, marching with the Guards' Brigade from Bloemfontein to Koomati Poort and back.

His dedication honors the officers and men for heroic daring and yet more heroic endurance. The narrative opens with the slide toward war in September 1899, as the Transvaal and Orange Free State broke with Britain. It gives readers a noncombatant's view of campaign life, endurance, and faith under fire.
25496-new-treasure-seekers-or-the-bastab:
E. Nesbit brings back the Bastable children for a fresh hunt for a fortune in this sequel to The Treasure Seekers. Oswald and his brothers and sisters travel farther afield, with early stories taking them on the road to Rome, into a stowaway scrape, and through a tangle called the conscience-pudding.

Each tale mixes practical scheming with comic failure, as the children's grand plans meet real trains, lodgings, grown-ups, and money troubles. Nesbit keeps Oswald's proud, matter-of-fact narration at the centre, letting young readers enjoy both the adventure and the gap between plan and result.
25566-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
The Northern Nut Growers Association records its fifteenth annual meeting, held in New York City on 3, 4, and 5 September 1924, in this proceedings volume. Officers, committees, state vice presidents, members, constitution, and by laws open the book.

Papers follow on top working hickories in the north, grafting at all times of year, stocks for hickories, and the search for blight resisting chestnut sprouts. Protection of wounds in nut trees, the nut situation in Iowa, and insects attacking northern nut trees show growers sharing practical trial results across states. The secretary's and treasurer's reports open the proceedings, followed by an address by Dr. Britton and reports from state vice presidents.
25597-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
The Northern Nut Growers Association records its seventh annual meeting, held in Washington, D. C., on 8 and 9 September 1916, printed at Annapolis. A modern disclaimer warns that articles state their authors' findings alone, not the association's endorsement, and that pesticide advice may have changed since writing.

Contents list officers, members, constitution and by laws, and the secretary treasurer's report. Papers on chinquapins and the black walnut open the proceedings. Other papers give growers of 1916 a shared record of trials, varieties, and orchard practice across the northern states. The volume preserves a young association's working record.
25675-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
The Northern Nut Growers Association records its fourteenth annual meeting at Washington, D. C., on 26, 27, and 28 September 1923, in this proceedings volume. Officers, state vice presidents, members, constitution, and by laws open the book.

The secretary's report leads the proceedings, followed by further notes on nut culture in Canada by Jas. A. Neilson. Addresses by Dr. L. C. Corbett and C. A. Reed follow, with commercial nut culture by T. P. Littlepage, notes by Mr. Bixby, and an address by Mrs. W. N. Hutt, showing growers sharing practice across borders. A modern disclaimer warns that articles state authors' findings alone.
25703-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
The Northern Nut Growers Association, affiliated with the American Horticultural Society, records its forty-fourth annual meeting at Rochester, New York, on 31 August and 1 September 1953, in this proceedings volume. Officers for 1953 to 1954 open the book.

A call to order, an address of welcome by Wilbur Wright, and secretary and treasurer reports lead the business. Papers cover blossoming habits of the Persian walnut. They cover the chestnut blight problem in Europe in 1953. They cover rooting chestnuts from softwood cuttings and chestnut breeding for 1953. A panel discussion on chestnuts and a Rochester attendance register close the record. Richard B. Best of Eldred, Illinois, served as president.
25775-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
The Northern Nut Growers Association records its thirteenth annual meeting at Rochester, New York, on 7, 8, and 9 September 1922, in this proceedings volume. Officers, state vice presidents, members, constitution, and by laws open the book.

The president's address leads the proceedings, with a biography of Dr. Walter Van Fleet and a letter on chestnut blight from G. F. Gravatt. Manchurian walnut industry, almond possibilities in eastern states, and opportunities for a woman in nut culture follow. The plane and screw in grafting, nut growing in the south, and the blight proof filbert show practical variety.
25799-the-girl-and-the-bill-an-american-:
Bannister Merwin writes The Girl and the Bill, an American story of mystery, romance, and adventure, published by Burt in New York in March 1909 with pictures. A man volunteering how puzzling letters were fronts the book.

Chapters open at the threshold of adventure, where State Street roars. Senhor Poritol, shadows, and the girl of the car follow. Evans, S. R., a chance lead, and a Japanese at large come next. The trail of Maku, number three forty-one, and find the American close the run, as a girl, a bill, and a mystery entwine in Chicago and beyond.
25831-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
The Northern Nut Growers Association records its thirty-seventh annual convention in this proceedings volume. Officers, state vice presidents, members, constitution, and by laws open the book, with a modern disclaimer that articles state authors' findings alone.

An address of welcome by Dr. J. H. Gourley, a response by John E. Cannaday, and an address by retiring president Carl Weschcke lead the business. Secretary Mildred M. Jones and treasurer D. C. Snyder report, followed by notes on the meeting, nut growing under semi-arid conditions, weather versus crops, and black walnut nursery studies.
25935-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
The forty third annual report of the Northern Nut Growers Association records its meeting at Rockport, Indiana, affiliated with the American Horticultural Society. A disclaimer warns that papers give their authors' views alone, not the association's, and that pesticide rules may have changed since writing. Growers remain bound by law to follow current label directions, and old results are no sure guide elsewhere.

Contents list a welcome, business session, treasurer's report, and a president's address by L. H. MacDaniels. Papers take up the future of nut planting, the value of a tree, and better crops on black walnut. A 1952 hickory survey, hickory stocks, filbert kinds, Chinese chestnuts, and Persian walnuts in the upper South and eastern Iowa follow. The report is a practical record of nut growers at work.
25992-the-martyrs-of-science-or-the-live:
Sir David Brewster tells the lives of Galileo, Tycho Brahe, and Kepler in The Martyrs of Science, printed by John Murray in 1841. Brewster, principal of the United College at St. Andrews and fellow of the Royal Society, dedicates the book to Lord Gray. He argues that science now gives nations power and wealth and warms the domestic hearth, so its votaries need no longer fear neglect or persecution.

Tycho's tale shows the old scorn: kin reproached him for leaving law, mocked his star watching as useless and degrading, and only his uncle Steno Bille praised his bent. Tycho quit his country for German cities, resumed watching at Wittenberg in April 1566, and fled plague to Rostock that autumn. Brewster writes of three star gazers who paid dearly for truth.
26013-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
The forty first annual report of the Northern Nut Growers Association records its meeting at Pleasant Valley, New York, affiliated with the American Horticultural Society. A disclaimer warns that papers give authors' views alone, not the association's, and that pesticide rules may have changed since writing. Growers remain bound by law to follow current label directions, and old results are no sure guide elsewhere.

Contents list a second day's session, the constitution, names, purposes, members, officers, directors, and by laws on membership and duties. One paper advises grub proofing lawns with chemicals once grubs reach five to ten per square foot, preferring chlordane at eight ounces of fifty percent powder per thousand square feet. The report is a practical record of nut growers, their rules, and their craft.
26105-the-oaths-signs-ceremonies-and-obj:
An 1868 exposé by a late member sets out the oaths, signs, ceremonies, and objects of the Ku-Klux-Klan. The writer hides his name, fearing the brothers of the Southern Cross, whose hatred and reach he describes as hound-like, already pressing into southern Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois.

Chapters recount his initiation, the consecrating bowl revealed as a human skull, and his detail with an older brother to form a new company in a neighboring county. Orders come from an unknown source through the captain, and the pair start the next night in obedience. With illustrations, the book offers the public a first inside account of the order's ritual and spread.
26455-a-history-of-lumsden-s-battery-c-s:
Written by Dr. George Little and James R. Maxwell and published by the R. E. Rhodes Chapter of the United Daughters of the Confederacy at Tuscaloosa, this history traces a Confederate artillery battery. Little covers its organization on November 4, 1861, through October 15, 1863, while Maxwell carries the story to its surrender on May 4, 1865. The authors wrote from memory in 1905, aided by a diary kept by Dr. James T. Searcy.

The narrative opens in May 1861, when Tuscaloosa men signed to volunteer after Judge Mudd announced a call from the bench. Some two hundred men joined within a week, under Captain Charles L. Lumsden, a Virginia Military Institute graduate. Camp anecdotes, portraits, and a roster of privates fill out a unit history told by its own veterans.
26667-the-strange-adventures-of-captain-:
George Augustus Sala published the first of three volumes of Captain Dangerous with Tinsley Brothers at London in 1863, dedicating it to sculptor Alexander Munro. Its hero was a soldier, a sailor, a merchant, a spy, and a slave among the Moors. He became a bashaw in the service of the Grand Turk, and ended his days in his Hanover Square house. Sala tells it as a narrative in old-fashioned English.

Volume One opens with Mine Own House and the history of an unknown lady who came from Dover in a coach-and-six. It continues with the history of the narrator's grandmother, who was a lady. Sala's preface contrasts eighteenth-century travel before steamers and railways, when a Grand Tour took years, with modern flying trips. The Fair Sophia, Madame Cottin's Elizabeth, and Scott's Jeanie Deans illustrate an age when going abroad meant staying abroad.
26668-the-strange-adventures-of-captain-:
George Augustus Sala attempted this narrative in old-fashioned English, publishing volume two with Tinsley Brothers at London in 1863. Its hero is John Dangerous. He was by turns a soldier, a sailor, a merchant, a spy, a slave among the Moors, and a bashaw in the service of the Grand Turk. He died at last in his Hanover Square house. Sala keeps the antique spelling and capitalization throughout.

Volume two follows Dangerous from going abroad and coming to man's estate through the Low Countries, the grand tour, and Paris, with a prison at Vienna on the way. Pressed into the fleet, he serves King George, sees rebellion ended, and goes into business on his own account. A miserly contractor, Sir Basil Hopwood, frames his boyhood, in a picaresque life told as if from the eighteenth century.
26669-the-strange-adventures-of-captain-:
George Augustus Sala published the third of three volumes of Captain Dangerous with Tinsley Brothers at London in 1863. This final volume carries its hero from seeing much of the world's inside and going right round it to secret service and slavery. He rises to a bashaw's rank, then comes home and buys his grandmother's house in Hanover Square, which is now his.

Its nine chapters cover Mercator and his projection, the voyage back to Europe, and singular misfortunes in Holland. A strange and horrible adventure in Paris nearly undid him. Secret employment under the Cardinal follows, then capture by recreant paynims and miserable slavery, and at last, after many surprising turns, J. Dangerous becomes Bestuschid Bashaw. The narrator opens in 1748, not yet forty, hale and stout, with a military education and a slender purse.
26844-borneo-and-the-indian-archipelago-:
Frank S. Marryat, late midshipman of the surveying ship Samarang, published this account of Borneo and the Indian Archipelago with Longman in 1848. Its heart is his large set of drawings of native dress and scenery, made during the ship's last surveying cruise. On his return they were judged fuller and more true to life than the hasty sketches survey officers usually managed. Marryat argues that the Admiralty should have supplied every survey ship with a trained draughtsman.

He had meant to publish the drawings alone, but was overruled, so he added letterpress drawn from his private journal and the journals of his messmates. The narrative follows the Samarang up Borneo's rivers, past mangroves and fortified towns, noting that few of the island's rivers run more than eighty miles. Drawings of costume and scenery carry the book's main claim.
27252-the-land-of-the-blessed-virgin-ske:
William Somerset Maugham's The Land of the Blessed Virgin, sketches and impressions in Andalusia, was published by Heinemann in 1905 and dedicated to Violet Hunt. It opens with the spirit of Andalusia and the churches of Ronda. The swineherd, Medinat Az-Zahra, the mosque, the court of oranges, and Cordova follow.

Seville brings the Alcazar, Calle de las Sierpes, Don Juan Tenorio, the women of Andalusia, the dance, a feast day, the Giralda, and the cathedral, before gaol and the bull-fight. Maugham holds that a traveller who falls in love with the country learns its language faster and sees its life sharper than the hotel-bound tripper.
27877-an-abridgment-of-the-architecture-:
Perrault's abridgment of the architecture of Vitruvius, first done in French by Claude Perrault and now Englished with additions, was printed in London in 1692 for Abel Small and T. Child. The volume contains a system of the whole works of Vitruvius, with copper plates and a table of explanation.

Chapters divide architecture into building, gnomonical, and mechanical parts, and into solidity, convenience, and beauty, listing the eleven things an architect should know, from geometry and history to music and law. The book carried classical architectural theory to English readers in the age of Wren.
28536-the-astronomy-of-the-bible-an-elem:
E. Walter Maunder of the Royal Observatory, Greenwich, wrote The Astronomy of the Bible as an elementary commentary on the astronomical references of Holy Scripture, published in 1908 with thirty-four illustrations. Maunder also wrote Astronomy Without a Telescope, and he dedicates this book to his wife, his helper in the book and in all things.

Chapters work through the Hebrew view of astronomy, creation, the deep, the firmament, the ordinances of the heavens, the sun, the moon, the stars, and comets. Maunder explains Hebrew words such as tehom and raqia, and contrasts Babylonian creation myth with Genesis. The book suits readers who want astronomy and Bible study together.
28719-fishing-in-british-columbia-with-a:
T. W. Lambert's Fishing in British Columbia, published by Horace Cox of London in 1907, adds a chapter on tuna fishing at Santa Catalina. Lambert, late surgeon to the Western Division of the Canadian Pacific Railway, writes from twelve years in the interior, fishing numberless lakes and streams. British Columbia grew easy of access only after the railway's completion in 1887, within two weeks' journey from London.

The country resembles Norway and Sweden in indented coast, pine forest, lake, and river, but with milder climate, richer valleys, and precious metals. Its population stands at one hundred thousand, against Scandinavia's ten millions. The rainbow trout, at home to the furthest north and bounded east by the Rockies, is the book's chief quarry.
28915-zigzag-journeys-in-northern-lands-:
Hezekiah Butterworth wrote this 1884 travel book, the fifth Zigzag volume, following the Zigzag Club from the Rhine to the Arctic. The summer trip runs through Holland, Germany, Denmark, Norway, and Sweden, teaching history by a supposed tour of interesting places. Butterworth, of the Youth's Companion staff, aimed to make German history, tradition, literature, and art live through stories and pictures of places.

The preface notes that over one hundred thousand Zigzag volumes had already sold, and that each volume stands complete by itself. Earlier Zigzag books covered Europe, classic lands, the Orient, and the Occident. Readers get a lively Victorian travel history for young people, with an illustration of carrying Siegfried's body, and a route that ends near the Arctic.
30471-betty-gordon-in-the-land-of-oil-or:
Alice B. Emerson sends Betty Gordon into oil country in a 1920 girls' series novel, subtitled The Farm That Was Worth a Fortune. It follows Betty Gordon at Bramble Farm and Betty Gordon in Washington, and stands beside Emerson's long Ruth Fielding series in the publisher's list.

Betty faces a farm whose value turns on oil, a setup that mixes home life, business, and adventure for young readers. Emerson keeps the plot lively and clear, with friends, rivals, and practical problems to solve. Illustrated and cloth bound, the book offers a wholesome heroine tale in which a girl's sense and courage matter as much as any fortune under the land.
30879-the-life-of-blessed-john-b-marie-v:
Compiled from approved sources, this life of Blessed John B. Marie Vianney, Curé of Ars, was published in New York by Joseph Schaefer, with a 1911 copyright. It carries a novena and litany to this zealous worker in the vineyard of the Lord, and it bears the Nihil obstat of Thomas B. Cotter and the imprimatur of John M. Farley, Archbishop of New York, dated October 22, 1910.

Its preface says spiritual reading has always been encouraged by the church, since it strengthens faith and stirs readers to devout practice. Against the materialistic tone of much modern literature, the preface argues, Catholic books are all the more urgent, since minds are moulded by reading. The life itself offers a devotional portrait of a parish priest, for Catholic readers seeking an example of pastoral zeal.
31031-guy-fawkes-or-a-complete-history-o:
The Reverend Thomas Lathbury, author of A History of the English Episcopacy from 1640 to 1662, wrote this complete history of the Gunpowder Treason of 1605, published in London by John W. Parker in 1839. Its full title adds a development of the principles of the conspirators and some notices of the Revolution of 1688. Lathbury presents Guy Fawkes and the dark design in a separate, full narrative.

His preface says the particulars may be read in general histories of the period, but no modern narrative of the design existed in separate form, only brief sketches in various works. He collected from various quarters all the information he could discover. He aimed at the most complete narrative of the treason ever published in detached form, yet concise enough not to weary the reader. It is a thorough Victorian history of the plot and its principles.
31072-a-letter-book-selected-with-an-int:
George Saintsbury's 1922 Letter Book pairs a full introduction on the history and art of letter-writing with a wide anthology of letters themselves. The introduction moves from ancient history through English letters before 1700, the eighteenth century, and the nineteenth century in two parts. It closes with special kinds of letters and a conclusion.

The selections range from Greek letters of Synesius and Latin letters of Pliny through the Paston letters, Roger Ascham, Lady Mary Sidney, John Donne, and many later writers. For readers and writers alike, the volume shows how the familiar letter grew from formal address into one of literature's most flexible and personal forms.
31089-the-subspecies-of-the-mexican-red-:
Keith R. Kelson wrote this paper on the subspecies of the Mexican red-bellied squirrel, Sciurus aureogaster. It was published in the University of Kansas Publications, Museum of Natural History, volume 5, number 17, pages 243 to 250, on April 10, 1952. Kelson starts from Nelson's 1899 treatment of the tree squirrels of Mexico and Central America, which recognized three subspecies of red-bellied squirrels.

They are Sciurus aureogaster aureogaster, Sciurus aureogaster hypopyrrhus, and Sciurus aureogaster frumentor. In his lists of specimens examined, Nelson assigned certain specimens from the mountains near Santo Domingo and Guichicovi in Chiapas, and from Catemaco in Veracruz, to aureogaster. Other specimens from the same localities went to hypopyrrhus. Kelson re-examines that tangled assignment. A subspecies is a local form of one kind of animal, set apart by small, steady marks. It is a careful revision of squirrel taxonomy.
31872-the-christian-church-in-these-isla:
The Reverend G. F. Browne's three lectures, delivered at St. Paul's in January 1894 and published in London the same year, trace the Christian church in these islands before the coming of Augustine. Browne, canon of St. Paul's and formerly Disney professor of archaeology at Cambridge, writes under the direction of the Tract Committee.

Lecture one covers Christianity in Kent before Augustine, Bishop Luidhard, Queen Bertha, and Romano-British churches in Canterbury, with legends of St. Paul, Joseph of Arimathea, and Glastonbury. Later lectures follow King Lucius, British bishops at councils, Pelagianism, and early Christianity beyond Kent. Readers get a scholarly introduction to Britain's first Christians.
31887-our-battery-or-the-journal-of-comp:
O. P. Cutter's 1864 journal Our Battery, or the Journal of Company B, 1st Ohio Volunteer Artillery was published at Cleveland. It was written hastily in camp leisure hours, with no thought of print, until companions-in-arms urged its publication. It is dedicated to Colonel James Barnett, commanding the First Ohio Artillery, a braver and kinder-hearted man to the soldier, in Cutter's words, than any other.

The journal begins under Lincoln's proclamation calling out troops for three years, with Company B, the second battery organized, departing Cleveland on September 4, 1861, amid relatives and friends at the depot. Readers get a firsthand artillery journal of the Civil War, unpolished and direct.
31969-eleven-days-in-the-militia-during-:
Eleven Days in the Militia During the War of the Rebellion, published in Philadelphia in 1883 by a militiaman, is a journal of the emergency campaign of 1862. Its introduction notes that twenty years have passed since a band of hastily gathered minute-men left their homes to defend Pennsylvania. They faced the first threatened invasion of the state by the rebel army under General R. E. Lee.

The author argues that, from their increasing remoteness, the incidents of that brief and comparatively unimportant campaign have taken on historic interest. They exceed the march of the celebrated Advance Light Brigade to defend Philadelphia in the War of 1812. Readers get a first-hand journal of citizen soldiers in September 1862.
32879-reflections-upon-two-pamphlets-lat:
A Lover of Truth reflects on two pamphlets lately published, printed in London for Richard Baldwin in 1693 with an imprimatur of April 21, 1693. The first is a letter from Monsieur de Cros concerning the Memoirs of Christendom. The second is an answer to that letter, pretended to have been written by the author of the Memoirs.

The reflector had hoped de Cros would move Sir William Temple, author of the Essay upon the Gardens of Epicurus, to take up his pen once more. After waiting two months he gave up hope. He calls de Cros's letter a sham of railing and foul language, fit to banter fools or children. He closes by asking forgiveness for his first essay, which may also be his last, and professing his passion for Temple's writings.
32995-our-caughnawagas-in-egypt-a-narrat:
Louis Jackson of Caughnawaga, captain of the contingent, wrote Our Caughnawagas in Egypt in 1885. It is a narrative of what the North American Indian voyageurs saw and did. They led the British boat expedition for the relief of Khartoum up the cataracts of the Nile. A preface by T. S. Brown explains that the Caughnawagas are an offshoot of the Mohawks, one division of the Six Nations, known to the French as Iroquois.

Jackson's account gives a first-hand view of river work under fire and strain, as Canadian voyageurs handled boats through rapids that British soldiers could not manage alone. The book is both a campaign memoir and a record of Indigenous skill put to imperial use. For readers of Canadian, military, and Indigenous history, it preserves a distinctive voice from a famous and difficult expedition.
33102-bloodletting-instruments-in-the-na:
Audrey Davis and Toby Appel's Bloodletting Instruments in the National Museum of History and Technology catalogues the museum's collection in 103 pages with 124 figures. It was published as Smithsonian Studies in History and Technology number forty-one in 1979. Its abstract notes that bloodletting, supported by a variety of instruments, became a recommended practice in antiquity. It remained accepted for millennia, punctuated by controversies over how much blood to take.

The study covers all major types of equipment and many variations, from lancets and scarificators to cups and leeches' tools, showing how a once-central therapy was practiced. Davis and Appel write as museum historians, letting objects tell the story of medicine's long confidence in bleeding. For historians of medicine and for museum visitors, the volume is a clear, well-illustrated guide to a practice now strange, but once ordinary.
33304-hair-breadth-escapes-the-adventure:
Rev. H. C. Adams's tale follows three boys through hair-breadth escapes in South Africa, a land the author knew from a visit made pleasant by kind hosts in Grahamstown. Dedicated to the principal of St Andrew's College there, the book recalls a journey full of narrow scrapes, wild country, and the quick thinking that saved its young heroes. Adams writes for boys who love adventure told with a clergyman's warmth.

The story moves from town to veld, with dangers that test courage and friendship at every turn. Its charm lies in its plain, hearty style and its affection for South Africa and its people. For readers who enjoy Victorian boys' books, Hair-Breadth Escapes offers a lively, wholesome adventure in a far-off land.
33346-how-to-tell-the-birds-from-the-flo:
Robert Williams Wood's How to Tell the Birds from the Flowers, copyrighted in 1917, is a revised manual of flornithology for beginners, in verse and woodcuts. Its contents pair birds with flowers that sound alike. The Crow goes with the Crocus, the Plover with the Clover, Ole Gander with Oleander, the Hen with the Lichen, and the Pelican with the Panicle. Wood's jokes turn confusion into delight.
